# 1 Kings Chapter 22 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** For three years there was no war between Aram and Israel.
**2** In the third year, King Jehoshaphat of Judah visited the king of Israel.
**3** The king of Israel said to his officials, "Don't you realize that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us? Yet we sit here doing nothing to reclaim it from the king of Aram."
**4** He asked Jehoshaphat, "Will you join me in attacking Ramoth-gilead?" Jehoshaphat replied, "Absolutely. My troops are your troops, my horses are your horses."
**5** But Jehoshaphat added, "First, let's ask the LORD for guidance."
**6** So the king of Israel assembled about four hundred prophets and asked them, "Should I attack Ramoth-gilead or not?" They all answered, "Attack! The Lord will hand it over to you."
**7** But Jehoshaphat asked, "Isn't there a prophet of the LORD we can consult?"
**8** The king of Israel told Jehoshaphat, "There is one more — Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him because he never prophesies anything good about me, only bad." Jehoshaphat said, "The king shouldn't say that."
**9** So the king of Israel called an officer and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once."
**10** The two kings, dressed in their royal robes, were sitting on thrones at the threshing floor near Samaria's gate, with all the prophets prophesying before them.
**11** Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made iron horns and announced, "This is what the LORD says: 'With these you will gore the Arameans until they are finished!'"
**12** All the prophets were saying the same thing: "Attack Ramoth-gilead and win! The LORD will hand it over to you."
**13** The messenger who had gone to get Micaiah told him, "Look, all the prophets are unanimously predicting success for the king. Just agree with them and say something positive."
**14** Micaiah said, "As surely as the LORD lives, I will say only what the LORD tells me."
**15** When he arrived before the king, the king asked, "Micaiah, should we attack Ramoth-gilead, or not?" Micaiah answered, "Oh, go ahead! Attack and win! The LORD will hand it to you."
**16** The king said, "How many times do I have to make you swear to tell me nothing but the truth in the LORD's name?"
**17** Then Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered across the hills like sheep without a shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These people have no leader. Send them home in peace.'"
**18** The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Didn't I tell you? He never has anything good to say about me — only bad."
**19** Micaiah continued, "Then listen to this word from the LORD. I saw the LORD seated on his throne with the entire heavenly army standing around him on his right and his left.
**20** The LORD asked, 'Who will lure Ahab to his death at Ramoth-gilead?' Various suggestions were made.
**21** Then a spirit stepped forward before the LORD and said, 'I'll do it.'
**22** 'How?' the LORD asked. The spirit said, 'I'll go and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.' The LORD said, 'That will work. Go and do it.'
**23** So understand — the LORD has put a lying spirit in all your prophets' mouths. The LORD has decreed disaster for you."
**24** Zedekiah son of Chenaanah walked up and slapped Micaiah across the face. "Since when did the LORD's Spirit leave me to speak through you?" he demanded.
**25** Micaiah replied, "You'll find out the day you're running from room to room trying to hide."
**26** The king of Israel ordered, "Arrest Micaiah! Take him to Amon the city governor and Prince Joash.
**27** Tell them, 'The king says: Lock this man up and put him on bread and water until I return safely.'"
**28** Micaiah declared, "If you ever return safely, the LORD has not spoken through me." Then he added, "Mark my words, everyone!"
**29** The king of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah marched to Ramoth-gilead.
**30** The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I'll go into battle in disguise, but you wear your royal robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle.
**31** Now the king of Aram had ordered his thirty-two chariot commanders, "Don't bother with anyone except the king of Israel."
**32** When the chariot commanders spotted Jehoshaphat, they thought, "That's the king of Israel!" and turned to attack him. Jehoshaphat cried out.
**33** When the chariot commanders realized it wasn't the king of Israel, they broke off their pursuit.
**34** But someone drew his bow at random and hit the king of Israel between the joints of his armor. Ahab told his chariot driver, "Get me out of here — I'm hit."
**35** The battle raged all day. The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans. He died that evening. Blood from his wound pooled in the bottom of the chariot.
**36** As the sun set, the cry went through the army: "Every man to his own town! Every man to his own land!"
**37** The king died and was brought back to Samaria, where he was buried.
**38** They washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria. The dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes bathed in it — fulfilling the word the LORD had spoken.
**39** The rest of Ahab's reign — everything he accomplished, the ivory palace he built, and all the cities he fortified — is recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
**40** Ahab died, and his son Ahaziah succeeded him.
**41** Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah in the fourth year of King Ahab of Israel.
**42** Jehoshaphat was thirty-five when he became king, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.
**43** He followed the example of his father Asa completely, doing what was right in the LORD's eyes. The high places, however, were not removed, and the people continued to offer sacrifices and burn incense there.
**44** Jehoshaphat was also at peace with the king of Israel.
**45** The rest of Jehoshaphat's reign — his achievements and military campaigns — is recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
**46** He rid the land of the remaining cult prostitutes who had survived from his father Asa's time.
**47** There was no king in Edom at that time; a governor ruled.
**48** Jehoshaphat built a fleet of trading ships to sail to Ophir for gold, but the ships never sailed — they were wrecked at Ezion-geber.
**49** Ahaziah son of Ahab offered to send his sailors with Jehoshaphat's, but Jehoshaphat refused.
**50** Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Jehoram succeeded him.
**51** Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He reigned two years.
**52** He did evil in the LORD's sight, following in the footsteps of his father, his mother, and Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin.
**53** He served and worshiped Baal and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, just as his father had done.
**54** [End of 1 Kings]

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

1. **22:8 — "I hate him because he never prophesies anything good"**: Ahab's complaint against Micaiah reveals everything wrong with his reign. He doesn't want truth — he wants comfort. A king who hates honest prophets will only hear liars.
2. **22:19-23 — the heavenly war room**: Micaiah pulls back the curtain on what's happening in heaven. God is on his throne, the angelic host is debating, and a spirit volunteers to deceive Ahab through his own prophets. The theology is staggering: even lies can serve divine purposes, and false prophecy can be permitted by a sovereign God.
3. **22:34 — "someone drew his bow at random"**: No one aimed at Ahab. A random arrow finds the one gap in his armor. This is the most precisely random event in the Bible — an accident that fulfills prophecy. You cannot hide from God's word by changing your clothes.
4. **22:38 — the dogs**: Elijah said it in chapter 21. Here it happens. Dogs lick Ahab's blood from the floor of his chariot. The Bible has a long memory, and prophecy always collects its debts.
5. **22:53 — the cycle continues**: 1 Kings ends as it began — with kings who do evil and prophets who confront them. Nothing is resolved. The story continues into 2 Kings, carrying its unfinished business with it.

— PNEUMA
